doc.title: Scott Jimmy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Living with the syndrome in silence
summary: He never discussed it with other kids or his brother; his mother told him to live with it, and he criticizes how little boys are taught.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were you teased by other children? Did they tease you?
No, no. I never discussed it with other kids.

Yeah, and I went on and actually didn’t learn about until I was much older. Then when I got much older, I began to realize, something is different, because my brother – my older brother would go to the bathrooom, and I’d say, “I got to go, too.” I’d run to the bathroom. He’d shut the door. I wouldn’t say anything, but I thought, why did you shut the door? I learned that that was why he shut the door. He didn’t want to discuss it with me, about the syndrome or anything. All I wanted from him was for him to be my brother. Just be my brother. Hey, that’s all. I never discussed it. I let it go, lived with it. My mother encouraged that, as far as living with it. She encouraged that in a lot of ways.
When you say she encouraged that, you mean she encouraged you to be hopeful and cope with what your reality was?
Because it’s going to be there.
There ain’t nothing you can do about it.
Nothing. That’s right. But like I say, every girl has – if they had boys – they had that syndrome. The first boy or the second boy.
The women in your family were the carriers.

Right. If they carried a baby, and if it was a boy, in the birth of that child, he had to live with the syndrome. But I feel that they’re wrong for what they do. They don’t teach them anything that will teach them anything that will help them understand what they’re living with. I think that’s so wrong, because it’s life.
And you have to be prepared . . .
There you go. To live it.
